calibration.note: A real Shopify B2C estimation, anonymised: 173 developer days (with code review, documentation, unit tests and bug fixing) and QA at 40% of them. Run on the same engagement’s recorded answers, the engine quotes 20–29.5 weeks, and the estimation at the team’s rate card falls inside that range.

pricing.$comment: Internal and never client-facing. A build week is what the delivery team does in one calendar week: the team above, 2.5 people full time, delivered offshore — front-end and back-end developers, QA, a project manager, a business analyst and a solution architect. weekly_rate is that week at the offshore rate card, converted from EUR at the ECB rate of 2026-09-23 (1 EUR = 0.939 CHF), rounded down; the rate card itself is not written here, because this repository is public. The shape comes from a real estimation (a Shopify B2C build of 173 developer days with QA at 40% of them, whose recorded answers the engine quotes at 20–29.5 weeks): developers 1.4, QA 0.55, and a project manager, business analyst and architect at 10, 10 and 7.5% of the delivery. Every modifier’s price is its weeks at this rate, so the quote is the Foundation base plus weeks a client can see. hypercare_rate_share: a week of hypercare after go-live — a named channel, a response within one working day, defects triaged — costs half a build week; each pack carries its own days (S 5, M 10, L 15 working days). app_weeks: each third-party app past what the pack includes (S 3, M 6, L 10) is an eighth of a build week, set so that crossing into a bigger pack, which includes more apps and more hypercare, never makes a quote cheaper. S.offer: New shop on a standard / custom theme

S.name: Ecommerce Foundation
S.for_whom: An established brand launching direct-to-consumer, or relaunching it properly — a retailer, a wholesaler or a label whose range already sells offline, in Switzerland first and in its languages. What it needs is a store that sells from day one, built the way a larger one would be, not a test of whether ecommerce works at all.
S.triggered_by: An estimate below the Scale floor: the Foundation, with whatever goes past it as add-ons
S.base_scope: A store that sells, on the shortest honest path · One market, one channel, one Shopify theme configured rather than rebuilt · The UI adapted to the brand identity by Merkle’s experience designer: tokens, typography, logo and the key screens · AI built in: the products listed for AI assistants — ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Meta, Google AI Mode and Gemini, and Shop — through Shopify Catalog, Shopify’s Knowledge Base app answering shoppers’ questions for the store, and Shopify Magic and Sidekick set up for the team · Sales channels connected: Shop, Google & YouTube, Facebook & Instagram and TikTok, with the catalogue synced, where each channel is available to the store · Native Shopify first, an app only where nothing native covers it · Core catalogue, standard checkout, the payment providers the market needs · A Merkle team with the quality gates of a larger build: accessibility and Core Web Vitals measured, not promised

scope_gates.condition: The requirements cannot be delivered on one store with Shopify Markets, so the engine's topology recommends expansion stores or a hybrid — or a second customer-facing brand needs its own store outright, regardless of market count. Shopify includes ten stores per Plus contract at no extra licence cost for genuine expansion stores of the same brand; a separate brand needs its own Plus subscription instead, which is why this is easy to agree to and expensive to deliver: expansion stores share no data by default, apps are billed per store and theme licences cannot be shared, so every integration is wired again, every theme deployed again and every app bought again, per store

platform_limit.note: A Plus contract carries one main store and nine expansion stores at no extra licence cost, and every expansion store must be identical to the main brand. The cost of a second store is not the licence: apps are billed per store, theme licences cannot be shared, and expansion stores share no data, so every integration is wired again.

scope_gates.label: Marketplaces
scope_gates.condition: The catalogue listed on marketplaces through Shopify Marketplace Connect — Amazon and eBay, and Target Plus and Walmart in the United States only; new Etsy connections cannot be made. Each marketplace is its own listing work: products mapped to its categories and attributes, prices and rules per marketplace, orders and stock tested both ways. Shopify’s own channels — Shop, Google & YouTube, Facebook & Instagram, TikTok — are configuration and in every pack.

scope_gates.label: Multi-currency
scope_gates.condition: More than one distinct checkout currency across markets whose price_strategy is not display_only

scope_gates.label: B2B / Wholesale
scope_gates.condition: B2B or hybrid business model (B2B selling unless answered otherwise), with B2B customer accounts, wholesale pricing, or volume discounts. Priced by what it asks of the store: Shopify’s own B2B set-up (standard), or catalogues per company, quote or negotiated pricing, a separate B2B storefront or checkout, or needs Shopify’s B2B does not cover (advanced)

scope_gates.label: Integration
scope_gates.condition: One or more live connections to a counted integration category (see integration_definition)

scope_gates.label: Storefront design
scope_gates.condition: The storefront needs more than theme configuration: bespoke sections or blocks from a key-screens design (extended), or a full template set from a mapped design system (bespoke). More bespoke sections than the offering builds is the full template set in all but name and prices as the bespoke tier. Horizon with brand tokens is in every offer and does not fire.

platform_limit.what: Sections per template or section group
platform_limit.note: Ours is the tighter number by a long way, and deliberately: the platform's 25 is what a template can hold, while 3 is what an offer builds before the work is a full template set. The engine reads merkle_line from here, so the page, the classifier and this file cannot disagree about it.

scope_gates.label: A second storefront design
scope_gates.condition: A market, channel or store needs a genuinely different storefront design — a different layout and page structure — rather than different content, imagery or translations. One design serves every market and every store in every pack, because Shopify's per-market customisation reaches section content, block visibility and order, and section-level settings — never theme settings and never Liquid templates: a genuinely different design is a second theme. The design system is not rebuilt — the second set is drawn against the same token layer — so this is the template work again, not the programme again. More than one customer-facing brand, each with its own full design system, is not this: that is Merkle Arc (rule 11.29).

scope_gates.label: Custom templates on a Shopify theme
scope_gates.condition: The storefront stays on a Shopify theme and needs page templates designed and built new — a campaign landing page, a lookbook, a product page for one range. Each is priced. A full template set from a design system is the bespoke storefront tier, which already designs and builds every template, so this is not priced on top of it. It is how a large, global set-up keeps a Shopify theme and still gets the pages it needs.

scope_gates.label: Headless storefront on Hydrogen
scope_gates.condition: A headless storefront is required and it is still a Shopify build: Hydrogen on the Storefront API, hosted on Oxygen, with content in Shopify. It is built instead of a Liquid theme and needs every template designed, so it carries the full template set with it: in S it replaces a configured theme with a React front end designed in full, in M it builds on the design days M already has for its templates, and in L it replaces the custom Liquid theme L builds anyway. The design system is created in Figma and tokenised by a design system architect, and the back end wires every query, hook and event a theme never needs. It is sold in every pack, and the engagement is named after the pack its budget reaches like any other. Content or a front end outside Shopify is Merkle Arc (rule 11.26).

scope_gates.label: Catalogue size and complexity
scope_gates.condition: Either arm fires it: 500 or more SKUs with complexity (two or more variant options, custom attributes, bundles or product sets), or 5,000 SKUs on their own whatever their shape — the point where Shopify stops showing filters on a collection and where the published benchmark moves from days of data work to weeks. Tiered by catalogue size, because the product model is built once and the data is handled per thousand

scope_gates.label: AI product content
scope_gates.condition: Product content written or enriched with AI across the whole catalogue before launch — descriptions, image alt text, the SEO title and meta description, attributes from supplier data into category metafields — in the brand’s voice, checked on a sample, approved by the client and loaded by product CSV. Shopify Magic already writes a description and suggests a category with its metafields as each product is edited, free: this is the same work for the whole catalogue at once. Product data only; no customer data reaches a model.

scope_gates.label: Search and merchandising
scope_gates.condition: Filtering and merchandising go past what Shopify Search & Discovery covers. Four documented limits, and the first two are the ones that decide scope: at most 25 filters per store, and a collection of more than 5,000 products shows no filters at all. The other two surface later and are the ones that surprise people — a single filter shows at most 100 values on the storefront, and a search returning more than 100,000 results shows no filters either

scope_gates.label: Migration
scope_gates.condition: Migration from any non-Shopify ecommerce platform (source_platform not none or shopify), e.g. Shopware, Magento, WooCommerce, SFCC, BigCommerce, custom

scope_gates.label: Returns and post-purchase
scope_gates.condition: What Shopify’s own returns do not do. Every pack sets up Shopify’s: customers request returns, and cancellations of items not yet shipped, from the order status page and staff approve them; return rules set the window, return shipping costs, a restocking fee and final-sale items, per market and per collection or product; staff add exchange items on approval; refunds go to the original payment or to store credit (new customer accounts only); delivery dates show at checkout. Standard is a returns or post-purchase app past that — return labels or QR drop-off outside the US (Shopify sells return labels only from US locations, for US domestic orders), refunds on the carrier’s first scan, customers editing their own orders, a branded tracking page with delivery updates by WhatsApp or push, warranty and repair claims. Advanced adds what the app has to reconcile with other systems: items inspected before the refund, and return and refund events passed to finance.

scope_gates.label: Retail & POS
scope_gates.condition: One or more physical stores sell with Shopify POS or an integrated POS, or omnichannel services are needed (pickup in store, ship from store, in-store returns of online orders, endless aisle, stock transfers, retail catalogs)

platform_limit.note: Apps that stock inventory — 3PL, dropshipping, custom fulfilment — are treated as locations but do not count toward the limit.

scope_gates.label: Languages
scope_gates.condition: 4 or more distinct languages across the markets — Translate & Adapt auto-translates two, and Swiss DE/FR/IT is included in every offer

scope_gates.label: SEO continuity
scope_gates.condition: The storefront's URLs change on a business whose traffic comes through search: significant SEO equity to preserve, a redirect estate of 1,000 URLs or more, or custom URL structures where organic is a priority channel. Deliberately independent of the migration gate — a rebuild on Shopify changes every URL without changing the platform. Shopify itself caps a store at 100,000 URL redirects, and 20,000,000 on Plus, so the ceiling that bites here is the work of building the map rather than the platform's

scope_gates.label: Subscriptions
scope_gates.condition: The store sells on a recurring basis: a subscription approach or features are recorded, subscription products are in the catalogue, or live contracts have to be carried across

scope_gates.label: Checkout extensibility
scope_gates.condition: The checkout needs more than its settings and the editor's branding. Three different things, and Shopify gates them differently: the Thank you and Order status pages take UI extensions on every plan except Starter; the information, shipping and payment steps take them only on Shopify Plus; backend logic is Shopify Functions — hiding, renaming or reordering payment methods by market, customer type or cart is a Payment Customization Function, not a setting. A fully custom checkout UI is exit rule 11.6, not this gate

scope_gates.label: Custom promotions
scope_gates.condition: A promotion Shopify’s own discounts cannot express — tiered or volume discounts for consumers (standard), or stacking rules of the business’s own across discounts (advanced) — built as a discount Function and owned as code. Codes, automatic discounts, buy X get Y, free shipping, scheduled sales and the native combinations are in every pack and do not fire this. Shopify documents tiered discounts, multi-step logic and custom eligibility as needing an App Store app, or on Shopify Plus a custom app of your own: a custom app containing a Function needs Plus, and a public App Store app runs on every plan.

scope_gates.label: Agentic commerce
scope_gates.condition: What takes a build past the AI every pack includes. Shopify’s agentic storefronts are active by default for eligible stores — ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Meta, Google AI Mode and Gemini and Shop read the products through Shopify Catalog — and every pack decides and sets them up, answers through the free Knowledge Base app and shows the team Shopify Magic and Sidekick. Standard is product data mapped from custom fields into the catalogue, and an AI crawler policy — robots.txt.liquid is an unsupported customisation where a mistake can lose all traffic. Advanced adds the store’s own shopping assistant or agent connection, on the store’s Storefront MCP endpoint and the Universal Commerce Protocol; the Universal Cart API is early access and is scoped, not promised.

scope_gates.label: Analytics and consent
scope_gates.condition: Measurement beyond what every store already has. Shopify Analytics — the pre-built reports, the dashboard and the ShopifyQL query editor — is on every plan, with more reports the higher the plan, and GA4 connects through the Google & YouTube channel with its ecommerce events tracked automatically. The gate opens past that: a third destination, a tag manager, custom events, server-side tagging or a third-party consent platform

scope_gates.label: Post-launch support
scope_gates.condition: An operating model past go-live: written SOPs the client’s team runs the store from, or a handover into a retainer other than a signed Grow retainer. Hypercare is not this gate: each pack carries its own days and more are priced by the week; launch-day training is in every offer; the handover into a signed Grow retainer is part of that retainer
scope_gates.$comment: No Shopify citation, deliberately: written SOPs and a handover into a retainer are how Merkle delivers, not something Shopify documents.

l_triggers.label: More than one Shopify store
l_triggers.condition: The engine's derived market topology (ai/engine/topology.js) recommends more than one Shopify store — a hybrid or a full expansion-store estate — because a business fact forces it: a selling entity per market beyond what Plus's own per-market entity assignment covers, its own tax and invoicing footprint, a genuinely different range, a market run by its own local team, a market needing its own theme design rather than shared content, a market with its own regulatory requirement, wholesale run as its own operation, or more than one customer-facing brand. Global reach alone never triggers this: Shopify documents no cap on markets per store, so an engagement selling in many markets from one Shopify Markets set-up stays whichever offer its other gates decide. It is recorded for the approach and the architecture and no longer decides the pack: each further store is priced by the store-estate gate, sold as an add-on on M and included in L up to three.

modifiers.description: Each further market with its own currency: Shopify Markets, Translate & Adapt, geo-routing, and the price list, rounding and payouts of its currency
modifiers.$comment: Only the storefront is surcharged. Languages are already priced per language and integrations per integration, so charging a market for them again would be the redirect estate mistake in another place: the same work billed twice because two rules each think they own it.

per_unit_surcharge.why: Bespoke sections are re-tested and signed off in every market, and nothing else charges for that
A full template set is re-tested and signed off in every market — the largest surface a further market meets

max_units.why: Shopify documents no cap on markets per store; twenty further markets, every one re-tested against a full template set, is where an estate stops being one build and rule 11.3 reads it as a programme

modifiers.description: Each Shopify store beyond the first: set-up, users, domain, tax and payments of its own, the theme deployed and kept in step, and every integration wired again per store — expansion stores share no data, so the more integrations there are, the more this costs per additional store; the apps are set up again in each store too, priced per app and store

per_unit_surcharge.why: No data is shared between stores, so every integration is wired, tested and reconciled again in each one — three integrations across the extra stores is three times the reconciliation work of one, not the same flat add-on regardless of count
Theme licences cannot be shared, so a bespoke template set is deployed and kept in step store by store

modifiers.$comment: Ten stores come with a Plus contract at no licence cost, which is exactly why nobody counts them. The cost is not the licence: it is apps billed per store, theme licences per store, and integrations wired per store because expansion stores share no data by default.

max_units.why: A Shopify Plus contract carries nine expansion stores; every one is charged, with three counted integrations (rule 11.7 stops a fourth) and a bespoke template set to redeploy

modifiers.description: Each marketplace listed through Shopify Marketplace Connect: products mapped to its categories and attributes, prices and listing rules per marketplace, and orders and stock tested both ways before it goes live.

max_units.why: Marketplace Connect lists on four marketplaces: Amazon, eBay, Target Plus and Walmart

modifiers.description: Shopify’s own B2B: company accounts, price lists, volume rules and payment terms
B2B past Shopify’s own set-up: catalogues per company, quote or negotiated pricing, a separate B2B storefront or checkout, or needs Shopify’s B2B does not cover
Bespoke sections and blocks built as Online Store 2.0 theme blocks from a key-screens design: schema, presets, translatable labels, Theme Check
A full template set from a mapped design system: every template, tokens wired to theme settings, motion and right-to-left where the markets need it

Each further storefront design, built from the client’s second design against the same token layer: its own theme installed, configured and Theme Checked, every template built again — more of them when the first design is a full template set — and the theme kept in step with the first on every release

per_unit_surcharge.why: A further design is built to the tier of the first: against a full template set every template is built again, which is most of a bespoke design’s own weeks

max_units.why: Shopify publishes one theme per store, so there is never a further design without a further store — nine at most

modifiers.description: Each page template designed and built new on a Shopify theme: the layout designed against the brand, built as sections and blocks the merchant can still rearrange, and tested on the real catalogue.

max_units.why: Past eight new templates the storefront is the full template set in all but name, and the bespoke tier of the storefront design gate prices it as one

modifiers.description: The storefront built as a React front end on Hydrogen instead of a Liquid theme, on top of the full template set it needs designed: the front end over a Liquid build of the same templates, and the back end a theme never needs — every query, hook and event wired to Shopify’s APIs.

parts.what: React front end, over a Liquid build of the same templates: the component library from the tokens, routes, server rendering and caching, locale routing per market, Oxygen environments and the deployment pipeline
Back end: Storefront API queries per template, cart and Customer Account API hooks, the content model read from metaobjects, cache revalidation on webhooks, and analytics events

modifiers.description: Each live connection to a counted system — ERP, PIM, CRM, OMS or 3PL
500 to 4,999 SKUs with complex variants, metafields or bundles: the product model designed once and applied

5,000 to 49,999 SKUs: the model is the same, the data is not — import batching, reconciliation per object, and the share of products that need a human before they load, with Search & Discovery set up for it
50,000 SKUs and above: catalogue operations in their own right — staged loads, a rehearsal run, and a data owner on the client side, with Search & Discovery set up for it

The catalogue’s content written or enriched with AI: a brand-voice guide and the prompts built from it, the attributes mapped to category metafields, generation across every product, a sample checked by people and approved by the client, and one product CSV import. A quarter of a build week per 1,000 SKUs, and three quarters at the least, which covers setting it up.

max_units.why: Fifty thousand SKUs is the very large catalogue tier; past it the content is a programme with its own owner, not a launch task

modifiers.description: Search & Discovery taken to its limits: the filter set designed against the product data that backs it, boosts and synonyms per collection, and a merchandiser who can change them afterwards
Past a documented Shopify limit, so a third-party search app: indexing and re-indexing, the sync that keeps it true, and the merchandising rules moved into it with an owner
The redirect map authored and imported, metadata and canonicals carried across, sitemap and indexation checked through cut-over
A redirect estate of 10,000 URLs or more, or rankings the business runs on: the map built from a crawl rather than a pattern, verified on staging, and indexation watched after launch
Shopify Subscriptions: selling plans, the storefront widget, the customer portal and the billing states the support team has to recognise
A third-party subscription app, or prepaid, build-a-box, B2B or international plans — and live contracts carried across without the customer re-entering a card, which is where these migrations fail
UI extensions on the Thank you and Order status pages — order tracking, surveys, referrals, an app block after the sale. Available on every plan except Starter, so this needs no Plus
UI extensions and custom fields on the information, shipping and payment steps. Shopify Plus only — on any other plan this is not a scope decision, it is a plan decision
Backend logic as Shopify Functions — validation, delivery or payment customisation, order rules: a deployed app with its own tests and release path, not a setting

One rule Shopify’s own discounts cannot express — tiered or volume discounts for consumers — as a discount Function with its rule table, unit tests on cart fixtures, thresholds a marketer changes without a deploy, and the storefront messaging that explains it.

Stacking rules of the business’s own across discounts: every rule written down against what the native combinations already cover, the remainder as a discount Function with its tests, configuration a marketer owns, and the cart and product-page messaging for each promotion.

Past the AI every pack includes: the product data that lives in metafields, metaobjects or titles mapped into Shopify Catalog as structured fields, and an AI crawler policy set in robots.txt.liquid, checked on the live domain before and after.

The store’s own shopping assistant, or the store connected to agent platforms, on top of the AI every pack includes: built on the store’s Storefront MCP endpoint — catalogue search, cart and the store’s policies — with the conversation designed, guardrails and an evaluation set the brand agreed, consent before any customer data reaches a model, and the model’s running cost named as the client’s, like an app’s fee.
Customer events, the destinations wired through them and consent respected on each — measurement that agrees with Shopify's own numbers
Server-side tagging or a third-party consent platform: consent state carried to every destination, capture points beyond checkout, and the reconciliation that proves the numbers still line up
One of the two: written SOPs, or a handover into a retainer that is not the Grow retainer — the runbooks and the owner named against each, past the launch-day training every offer carries
Both: a documented operating model the client’s team runs the store from, handed into a retainer that has to receive it, with a training programme behind it

A returns or post-purchase app past Shopify’s own returns: configured to the client’s policy, labels or QR drop-off with the carriers the client uses, the return portal and tracking page branded to the storefront, delivery updates on the channels asked for, warranty claims where they are in scope — tested on real orders and handed over with an owner.

The standard work, and the app reconciled with the systems around it — half a week to a week more: items inspected in the warehouse before the refund is released, and every return, refund and cancellation passed to finance with a daily check that the two agree. The connection to the ERP itself is the integration add-on.
Each location selling with Shopify POS: hardware, inventory, staff and the in-store test pass
WooCommerce or Shopify-to-Shopify: catalogue, customers and order history. The redirect estate is the SEO continuity gate, not this one.
Shopware or BigCommerce: data model differences to map, order history, customer and price-list structures. Redirects are priced by the SEO continuity gate.
Magento, Salesforce Commerce Cloud or a custom platform: a bespoke data model to map and integrations to re-point. Redirects are priced by the SEO continuity gate.
Price lists, rounding, payout and reconciliation per currency — priced on its own only where one market sells in several currencies; a further market carries its own
Each language beyond the third: translation of products, collections, policies, URL handles, theme and app strings — and again on every release

integration_definition.note: An integration is a live system-to-system data connection. Shopify App Store apps with native connectors (ESP, reviews, search, loyalty, analytics) are apps, not integrations — unless the connector is custom-built (connector = custom), in which case they count.

exit_results.STOP: Beyond the S/M/L offers. Not a refusal: the engagement continues as a Larger Engagement with a consultant-led Discovery Phase, or Merkle does not bid. Recorded in Q10.5.5 before the closing document.
exit_results.FLAG: Does not block GO. Requires a named owner and resolution before build starts.
exit_results.WARN: Commercial point for the proposal, kept out of every client section. Does not block GO.

exit_rules.condition: A required Shopify feature needs a higher plan than the target plan, per Shopify's plan documentation (Plus: company-specific or more than 3 B2B catalogs, B2B deposits and partial payments, checkout step extensions / Checkout Branding API, expansion stores, several legal entities, combined listings, Multipass sign-in, more than 10 locations, more than 20 languages, several product discounts on one item; Advanced: B2B contextual experience, per-market customisation, carrier-calculated rates, multi-currency payouts, more than 5 staff users; Grow: A/B testing with Rollouts). Shopify B2B itself runs on every plan from Basic. A fully custom checkout UI is handled by 11.6, not here
exit_rules.destination: Confirm the plan the requirements need, or remove the feature from scope
exit_rules.label: A requirement needs a higher Shopify plan than the one we are quoting

exit_rules.condition: B2B requires request-for-quote or prices negotiated per buyer (Shopify has no built-in RFQ)
exit_rules.destination: B2B architecture review: Shopify B2B draft-order review or a quote app (App Store category "Pricing quotes"), before build
exit_rules.label: B2B needs quotes or prices negotiated per buyer, which Shopify has no built-in way to do

exit_rules.condition: Scope has outgrown the gate work the largest pack carries — Ecommerce Flagship’s band spans nine to nineteen weeks of scope gates — AND two or more delivery risks are still open (no connector or iPaaS, a migration carrying rankings, a deadline shorter than the build, an unsettled store topology, a system with no test environment). Size alone is not a programme: every gate is quoted at its own weeks and price. What cannot be quoted is scope this large that cannot yet be committed to
exit_rules.destination: An Enterprise Engagement opening with a dedicated Discovery Phase, to close the open risks before the scope is committed
exit_rules.label: Scope past the largest pack, with too much about delivering it still open

exit_rules.condition: More than 6 distinct languages across all markets
exit_rules.destination: Larger Engagement: translation and content operations in the Discovery Phase
exit_rules.label: More than six languages across the markets

exit_rules.condition: More than 3 variant options per product (Shopify limit), or more than 2,048 variants on one product
exit_rules.destination: Product model review: combined listings, a product options app for non-stock options, or splitting products
exit_rules.label: More product options or variants than Shopify allows on one product

exit_rules.condition: Fully custom checkout UI — not possible on Shopify (checkout.liquid is retired; only Checkout Extensibility)
exit_rules.destination: Merkle Arc — composable commerce, scoped separately
exit_rules.label: A fully custom checkout, which Shopify no longer permits

exit_rules.condition: More than 3 integrations at launch (counted per integration_definition)
exit_rules.destination: Larger Engagement: integration architecture in the Discovery Phase
exit_rules.label: More than three systems connected at launch

exit_rules.condition: Regulated industry (pharma, alcohol, firearms, age-restricted, financial products, medical devices)
exit_rules.destination: Legal / compliance review
exit_rules.label: A regulated industry — pharma, alcohol, firearms, age-restricted, financial or medical

exit_rules.condition: PCI scope beyond Shopify-hosted payments (custom card UI, tokenisation, handling card data)
exit_rules.destination: Security review (threat model mandatory)
exit_rules.label: Card data handled outside Shopify’s own payment pages

exit_rules.condition: GDPR / CCPA data export or deletion workflow required
exit_rules.destination: Legal sign-off on data-subject request handling
exit_rules.label: Customers must be able to export or delete their data on request

exit_rules.condition: An M or L engagement with no Grow retainer agreed yet
exit_rules.destination: Offer the Grow retainer — run, optimise and the Phase 2 roadmap — and record the client’s answer before build starts. Its price is kept open
exit_rules.label: An M or L engagement with no Grow retainer agreed yet

exit_rules.condition: ERP or PIM with no existing Shopify connector and no iPaaS
exit_rules.destination: Integration scoping as its own track, before the build is quoted
exit_rules.label: An ERP or PIM with no ready-made Shopify connector and no integration platform in place

exit_rules.condition: fulfilment_locations > 2 AND routing beyond Shopify's native order routing rules (a custom routing Function or the ERP / OMS decides)
exit_rules.destination: Multi-location inventory scoped separately
exit_rules.label: More than two fulfilment locations, with routing Shopify cannot do on its own

exit_rules.condition: Migration with significant SEO equity or complex historical data
exit_rules.destination: Dedicated migration scoping track — not combined with the store build sprint
exit_rules.label: A migration carrying real search traffic or complex history

exit_rules.condition: Weeks from kick-off (delivery.kickoff_date, else meta.created_at) to target go-live are fewer than the offer's minimum duration_weeks
exit_rules.destination: Re-scope to an MVP-first delivery before any sprint begins
exit_rules.label: Less time to go-live than the offer needs

exit_rules.condition: No single decision-maker, or budget approval authority is unclear
exit_rules.destination: Named client decision-maker and budget owner confirmed before the statement of work is signed
exit_rules.label: No single decision-maker, or unclear budget authority

exit_rules.condition: Sensitive personal data is collected (health, age, biometric or financial data; special-category data under GDPR art. 9)
exit_rules.destination: Data protection impact assessment and legal sign-off on data minimisation, storage location and consent before build
exit_rules.label: Sensitive personal data — health, age, biometric or financial

exit_rules.condition: Existing Shopify store uses retired or deprecated features (Shopify Scripts, checkout.liquid / additional scripts, online store script tags, legacy customer accounts, Stocky, Geolocation app)
exit_rules.destination: Deprecation migration scoped as its own workstream (e.g. Scripts to Functions, legacy to customer accounts)
exit_rules.label: The existing store runs on Shopify features that are being retired

exit_rules.condition: B2B requirement that Shopify B2B does not support (subscriptions, local delivery or pickup points, express checkouts, more than 500 line items, gift cards)
exit_rules.destination: B2B architecture review: app or process change before build
exit_rules.label: A B2B requirement Shopify’s own B2B does not support

exit_rules.condition: Mainland China (CN) is a launch market. Selling onshore behind the Great Firewall needs a PRC entity, an ICP filing or licence and onshore hosting, and Shopify has no infrastructure in mainland China; cross-border routes (marketplaces, mini-programs, a Hong Kong store) have their own customs and product rules. Not part of the Merkle offering: CN is excluded from this engagement's markets, languages, offer, plan and build scope
exit_rules.destination: A separate China discovery — see the China note
exit_rules.label: Mainland China is one of the launch markets

exit_rules.condition: Mainland China is the only launch market — not part of the Merkle offering
exit_rules.destination: A separate China discovery — see the China note
exit_rules.label: Mainland China is the only launch market

exit_rules.condition: More than 5 retail stores in scope
exit_rules.destination: Quote the retail roll-out as a programme with roll-out increments, or as a rate-carded run team
exit_rules.internal_note: Above five locations, never quote a per-store price: a store with its own line item gets compared to 40 hours. Quote the programme and its increments, or a rate-carded run team (never shown to the client)
exit_rules.label: More than five retail stores in scope

exit_rules.condition: More than one market AND the topology inputs are materially unresolved: more than one legal entity recorded with no per-market entity mapping, or the assortment relationship per market unknown, or the invoicing and tax-registration footprint unknown. Fires on missing facts, not on a missing decision — the engine still recommends a topology.
exit_rules.destination: Market topology and legal-entity mapping workshop before the solution architecture is baselined.
exit_rules.label: Several markets, with the legal entities and pricing still unresolved

exit_rules.condition: A system Merkle has to build a connector for has no non-production environment to integrate against (test_environment none). Shopify itself needs no instance ladder — a theme stages as an unpublished theme in the production store and checkout is managed — so the only environment risk on a Shopify build sits on the client side. Without a sandbox, integration testing serialises against the client’s live system and the schedule stretches
exit_rules.destination: A named owner on the client side and a decision before the build starts: provide a sandbox, or agree the testing window against production
exit_rules.label: A system to be connected has no test environment to build against

exit_rules.condition: A headless storefront on a plan below Shopify Plus. Oxygen storefronts always have a production and a preview environment and custom ones besides, but only one environment can be public: the limit is 1 on Starter, Basic, Grow and Advanced against 25 on Plus. Every other deployment needs a login to the store, which constrains how many review links can run in parallel with client stakeholders
exit_rules.destination: A named owner before the build starts: agree who reviews where, or price the Plus plan
exit_rules.label: A headless storefront below Plus, where only one deployment can be public

exit_rules.condition: The storefront leaves Shopify: editorial content is managed in an external CMS or PIM rather than in Shopify metaobjects, or the front end is not a single Hydrogen storefront — another framework, a native app, or several front ends on one backend. exit_rules.condition: One order delivered to more than one address — gifting to several recipients, or a wholesale buyer splitting a single order across branches. Shopify has no way to do this: split shipping divides an order into several shipments when items cannot travel together, but every shipment goes to the same address, and it does not apply to accelerated checkouts or to draft orders that already carry a shipping line
exit_rules.destination: Decide before the build: one order per address, an app that does it, or drop the requirement — and say which in the proposal

exit_rules.condition: A presence inside Shopify's Shop app — a Shop Mini. Publishing one also needs Manage apps permission in the Partner organisation. None of these offers estimates React Native work
exit_rules.destination: Not included in S, M or L: scope and price the Mini separately, and agree whether it runs in this engagement or after it
exit_rules.label: A Shop Mini — a build these offers do not price

exit_rules.condition: More than one customer-facing brand, each needing its own design system — its own tokens and components (Q9.2.14). Brands that share one design system stay in the offers: a store per brand (an add-on on M, up to three in L) and a further storefront design where a brand’s layout differs. A design system per brand is a design programme, not a pack
exit_rules.destination: Merkle Arc — a design-system programme per brand, scoped by the Arc practice
exit_rules.label: More than one brand, each with its own design system

routes.label: Larger Engagement
routes.proposal: Merkle Enterprise Engagement with a dedicated Discovery Phase
routes.description: The requirements go beyond the S/M/L offers. This is not a refusal and not a pause: Merkle proposes an Enterprise Engagement that opens with a full, consultant-led Discovery Phase — a traditional discovery, run by people rather than by this tool. The approach drafted here is its starting point, and the client deck is produced and shared with the client as it would be for any engagement. What is not produced is the Jira backlog and the Confluence pages: the backlog is defined during that Discovery Phase, and issuing one now would imply a scope nobody has agreed.

routes.label: Merkle Arc
routes.proposal: Merkle Arc — a separate engagement, scoped by the Arc practice
routes.description: Beyond these three offers is Arc: Merkle’s enterprise platform for unifying brand design, content and commerce in one architecture — a tokenised design system, a multi-channel component library, GraphQL middleware and its own console, composable and headless without the vendor lock-in. A storefront that is not a Shopify theme, and a design system that is the design source rather than a brand to apply, are Arc’s shape rather than an offer’s. Nothing here quotes it, estimates it or drafts a Shopify approach for it: this engine prices Shopify builds. What goes across is the discovery — every answer, every requirement and the STOP that named the reason.

closed_scope.$comment: What each pack sells, closed. Every row is checked against the engine by a test: an engagement that takes exactly what a pack promises must classify as that pack, and its scope gates must fit inside the weeks that pack's band already carries. Anything past a row is quoted on top of the pack, never assumed into it. `limits` is the machine-readable form of the same promise and is what the test builds from. Rows are the comparison table: a pack includes something of every row, and a cell is the most that pack holds — a quantity, or an em dash where the pack holds none of it, never an explanation. A capability no pack includes is not a row at all: it is an add-on service, listed in `addons` with its scope and its cost. `groups` is the reading order of the row groups.

rows.shopify_limit: No documented cap on markets per store
rows.L: Up to 9 markets, across its stores
rows.note: The most the pack holds with everything else in it taken too. A further market is three quarters of a week, and a third more where it meets a bespoke template set rather than a configured theme — a market is re-tested and signed off against whatever the pack builds, so it costs more in the larger packs than in the entry one. What it costs in each pack is on the add-on services page.

rows.shopify_limit: One store per subscription; a Plus contract carries ten — one main store and nine expansion stores, each of which must be identical to the main brand
rows.note: One store already serves every market in the pack — a different currency, language, domain, price and catalogue per market, no second store required. When the requirements do need a second store it is an add-on on M, and L includes up to three. Each further store is its own set-up, domain, tax and payments, the theme deployed again and every integration wired again, because expansion stores share no data. Whether the requirements need one is not a question we ask: the engine derives it from the market answers — does another market invoice through its own company, hold its own tax registration, sell a genuinely different range, run under its own team, need its own theme design, or belong to a second brand.

rows.shopify_limit: Shop lists eligible stores where Shopify Payments is supported; Google & YouTube is available in certain countries and currencies and needs a Merchant Center account; Facebook & Instagram is free on every plan, subject to eligibility

rows.M: Shop, Google & YouTube, Facebook & Instagram and TikTok connected, with the catalogue synced
rows.L: Shop, Google & YouTube, Facebook & Instagram and TikTok connected, with the catalogue synced

The channel apps are made by Google, Meta and TikTok, and a channel’s own ads are the client’s. Marketplaces are listing work per marketplace — the marketplaces add-on.

rows.shopify_limit: Assigning a business entity per market is Shopify Plus only, and needs Shopify Payments and the new Markets
rows.note: Every pack assumes one selling entity, because a second is a plan decision before it is a scope one (rule 11.1). Past what Plus’s own per-market entity assignment covers, a further entity is a further store — the row above. Several markets with the entities and the tax footprint still unresolved is a flag of its own (rule 11.23).

rows.shopify_limit: Charging in a local currency needs Shopify Payments or Adyen; with any other provider the buyer is charged in the store’s default currency

rows.note: Translate & Adapt auto-translates two and Swiss DE/FR/IT is in every pack, which is why the gate opens at the fourth. Six is the ceiling in every pack: more is a separate discovery (rule 11.4), well below what Shopify itself would publish.

rows.shopify_limit: Shopify Tax covers the United States, European Union, United Kingdom and Canada; Basic Tax covers Norway, Switzerland, Australia, New Zealand and Singapore and needs a tax registration number. Shopify calculates, and never files or remits
rows.note: The same set-up work in every pack, scaled by the markets row rather than priced on its own. The registrations themselves are the client’s to hold — no configuration works around one they do not have — and the rates, duties and thresholds are completed in the configuration workbook once the pack is agreed (ADR 0012).

rows.shopify_limit: 3 variant options and 2,048 variants per product; above 5,000 products a collection shows no filters at all

rows.M: Up to 4,999 SKUs, with complex variants, metafields or bundles
rows.L: Up to 4,999 SKUs, with complex variants, metafields or bundles
rows.note: Five thousand is not an arbitrary line: above it Shopify shows no filters on a collection, so a catalogue that size brings the search row with it and costs a week more than the catalogue work alone. That is why it is an add-on rather than a bigger pack. A product needing more options or variants than Shopify allows is its own review (rule 11.5).

rows.shopify_limit: 25 filters per store (25 on Plus too), at most 100 values shown per filter, no filters on a collection above 5,000 products or on a search returning more than 100,000 results

rows.M: Shopify Payments or a gateway, with the market’s local methods
rows.L: Shopify Payments or a gateway, with the market’s local methods

rows.S: Shopify’s own discounts: codes and automatic, amount or percentage off, buy X get Y, free shipping, scheduled sales, native combinations
rows.M: Shopify’s own discounts: codes and automatic, amount or percentage off, buy X get Y, free shipping, scheduled sales, native combinations

rows.note: Locations and their routing rules are configuration in every pack. More than two fulfilling locations with routing Shopify cannot do on its own is scoped separately (rule 11.13), and more than ten locations is a plan decision (rule 11.1). Selling in a physical store with Shopify POS is not this row — it is an add-on service.

rows.shopify_limit: Flat, weight-based and price-based rates from Basic; live third-party carrier-calculated rates need Advanced or Plus, and a paid add-on on Grow
rows.S: Rate tables — flat, weight or price
rows.M: Rate tables — flat, weight or price
rows.L: Rate tables — flat, weight or price
rows.note: The shipping profile is set up for the markets in scope in every pack. The rates themselves, the free-shipping thresholds per market and the delivery methods are completed in the configuration workbook once the pack is agreed (ADR 0012). Live carrier-calculated rates are a plan decision (rule 11.1); one order delivered to more than one address is something Shopify cannot do at all (rule 11.27).

rows.shopify_limit: Return labels are sold in Shopify only from US fulfilment locations, for US domestic orders; store credit needs new customer accounts
rows.S: Shopify’s own returns: requests from the order status page approved by staff, return rules per market and product, exchanges added on approval, refunds to the original payment or store credit
rows.M: Shopify’s own returns: requests from the order status page approved by staff, return rules per market and product, exchanges added on approval, refunds to the original payment or store credit

rows.shopify_limit: No documented cap on connected systems — Shopify limits the rate of Admin API calls per store instead
rows.note: A system integration is a live connection to an ERP, PIM, CRM, OMS, 3PL/WMS or POS — or any other system wired with a custom connector. An App Store app that already talks to Shopify natively (email, reviews, search, loyalty, analytics) is not one, whichever pack it is in. One is what the band carries with everything else in the pack taken too; each further one is quoted on top, and more than three at launch is a separate discovery (rule 11.7).

rows.shopify_limit: No documented Shopify ceiling — what sets the work is the source platform’s data model
rows.note: The tier is set by where the data comes from, because that is what decides the work: WooCommerce and Shopify share a data model, Shopware and BigCommerce do not, and Magento, SFCC and bespoke platforms need the model mapped and every integration re-pointed. Ecommerce Scale carries the two that share Shopify’s model; everywhere else a migration is quoted on its own, because a replatform is a project with its own shape and absorbing it into a band prices it by accident. The redirect estate is not in here — it is the SEO continuity row, priced once. A migration carrying real search traffic or complex history is scoped as its own track (rule 11.14).
rows.addon_label: Every platform in S and L; Shopware, BigCommerce, Magento, Salesforce Commerce Cloud or a custom platform in M

rows.shopify_limit: Shopify Analytics is on every plan, with more pre-built reports the higher the plan
rows.S: Shopify Analytics, its reports, and GA4’s own ecommerce events
rows.M: All of that, plus events per market and currency, or from an app
rows.L: All of that, plus a custom GA4 event implementation
rows.note: Every store already has Shopify Analytics: the pre-built reports, the dashboard and the ShopifyQL query editor. GA4 connects through the Google & YouTube channel and its ecommerce events are tracked automatically — that is S, and it is not a small thing. Ecommerce Scale adds the events a multi-market store needs that the standard set does not carry, and the events an app emits. Ecommerce Flagship adds an event layer designed against what the client actually measures. The add-on is what goes past that in any pack: a third destination, a tag manager, server-side tagging or a consent platform. Shopify’s own cookie banner is configured for every market in scope in every pack: Shopify switches it on automatically only for the UK and the EEA, so a Swiss store gets it because someone set it up.
rows.addon_label: More destinations, a tag manager or consent

rows.shopify_limit: 5 staff accounts on Grow, 15 on Advanced, unlimited on Plus; Basic has none. Collaborator and POS-only accounts are not counted
rows.note: Users, roles and permissions are set up in every pack, one set per role rather than one shared login — per market in Ecommerce Flagship. The headcount is a plan gate rather than a licence add-on and can move the store up a plan on its own (rule 11.1), which is why it is counted before the plan is quoted.

rows.M: Native first, then an app — installed and owned
rows.L: Native first, then an app — installed and owned

The allowance is the first store’s: in every further store each app is installed and configured again, and priced on top. Each further app is bought on top too. The apps’ own monthly fees are the client’s.

rows.$comment: A Merkle line, not a Shopify fact: how many App Store apps a pack installs, configures and hands over with an owner and a monthly cost.
rows.note: Shopify’s own apps — Translate & Adapt, Search & Discovery, Flow, Forms, Subscriptions — do not count, and neither does an app a scope gate already prices. Each further app is bought on top. The apps’ own monthly fees are the client’s.

rows.$comment: No Shopify citation, matching the gate: hypercare, training and written SOPs are how Merkle delivers, not something Shopify documents.
rows.note: A named channel, a response within one working day and defects triaged with the client, for the working days each pack carries after go-live — per market where the launch is phased. More days are bought by the week. Training per role on the day-to-day is in every pack too. Written SOPs or a handover into a retainer are quoted on top.

addons.note: Sold on M, and included in L up to three stores. One store already serves every market; a second is needed only when the requirements force it, which the engine derives from the market and brand answers. Each further store is its own set-up, users, domain, tax and payments, the theme deployed and kept in step, and every integration wired again — expansion stores share no data. Below Shopify Plus every store carries its own plan; a Plus contract includes nine expansion stores of the same brand. Every app the store runs is installed and configured again in each further store, priced per app and store.

A further market brings its own currency and is priced as one market: a second currency is charged on its own only where a single market sells in several.

The same build whichever pack it sits in, so it is priced the same way in all three rather than folded into the largest. Wholesale only is not this: that is the base of the pack, the same weeks spent differently.

Quotes or prices negotiated per buyer are an architecture review, because Shopify has no built-in way to do them (rule 11.2).

addons.what: Bespoke sections, or a full template set
addons.description: The storefront past theme configuration: bespoke sections and blocks built from a key-screens design, or every template built from a mapped design system over one token layer.

addons.note: Sold where a further store is: on M with the store add-on, and in L. Shopify publishes one theme per store, and per-market customisation reaches section content, block visibility and order, and section-level settings — never theme settings or Liquid templates — so a genuinely different layout is a second theme on a second store. Built from the client’s second design against the same token layer: the design system is not built twice. More than one brand, each with its own design system, is Merkle Arc instead (rule 11.29).

addons.what: Each custom template on a Shopify theme
addons.description: A page template designed and built new — a campaign landing page, a lookbook, a product page for one range — while the storefront stays on a Shopify theme rather than a custom one. How a large, global set-up keeps its theme and still gets the pages it needs.
addons.note: A custom theme includes it: the full template set designs and builds every template, so this is priced only where the storefront stays on a Shopify theme — in L, instead of the custom theme. Past eight templates the full template set is the better buy. Shopify allows 1,000 JSON templates per theme.

addons.description: The storefront built as an owned Hydrogen front end on Oxygen instead of a Liquid theme, with the design system created in Figma and tokenised by a design system architect alongside the experience designer. Content stays in Shopify, in metaobjects and metafields.
addons.note: Sold in every pack, and not the same work in each: in S it replaces a configured theme with a React front end designed in full, in M it builds on the design days M already has, and in L it replaces the custom Liquid theme — the designer designs either way. It brings the full template set with it. The engagement is named after the pack its budget reaches. Content or a front end outside Shopify is Merkle Arc (rule 11.26).

addons.what: A larger or more complex catalogue
addons.description: A catalogue past what the pack carries. The product model is designed once; the data is handled per thousand — import batching, reconciliation per object, and the share of products that need a human before they load.

Descriptions, image alt text, SEO fields and attributes from supplier data, written or enriched with AI for the whole catalogue in the brand’s voice, checked on a sample, approved by the client and loaded in one import.
addons.note: Shopify Magic does this product by product in the admin, free, and stays available to the client’s team. Product data only: no customer data reaches a model. Translating the content is the languages add-on.

addons.what: Search past a documented Shopify limit
addons.description: Search & Discovery taken to its documented limits, or a third-party search app where the filter set or the catalogue goes past them — indexing, the sync that keeps it true, and the merchandising rules moved into it with an owner.
addons.note: At 5,000 SKUs and above the catalogue add-on already sets up Shopify’s own search; a search app past it is priced here.

addons.what: Migration from another platform, priced by source
addons.description: Priced by where the data comes from: light (WooCommerce), medium (Shopware, BigCommerce, an unnamed platform), heavy (Magento, Salesforce Commerce Cloud, a custom platform). Ecommerce Scale already carries a WooCommerce or Shopify migration; every other source, and any migration in S or L, is quoted by its tier beside the pack.

addons.what: Returns and post-purchase, past Shopify’s own
addons.description: A returns or post-purchase app where Shopify’s own returns stop — labels outside the US, refunds on the carrier’s scan, customers editing orders, a branded tracking page, warranty claims — and, advanced, reconciled with the warehouse and finance.
addons.note: Shopify’s own returns are in every pack: requests from the order status page approved by staff, return rules per market and product, exchanges added on approval, refunds to the original payment or store credit. The app’s own monthly fee is the client’s.

addons.description: Each location selling with Shopify POS: hardware, inventory, staff and the in-store test pass — and the omnichannel services that come with it, such as pickup in store, ship from store and in-store returns of online orders.
addons.note: Up to five locations. Above that it stays in the offer with a named owner and is quoted as a roll-out programme or a rate-carded run team rather than per store (rule 11.22). Shopify allows ten inventory locations per store and 200 on Plus, so past ten it is also a plan decision (rule 11.1).
L already carries six languages, and a seventh is a separate discovery (rule 11.4), so this is sold on S and M.

addons.what: SEO continuity: a redirect estate of 1,000 URLs or more, or rankings the business runs on
addons.description: The redirect map, the metadata and the canonicals carried across a URL change. Up to ten thousand URLs the map is authored from the old estate’s patterns and imported, with indexation watched through cut-over (standard); above that, or where the business runs on its rankings, it is built from a crawl, verified on staging and watched after launch (large). Below a thousand URLs the redirects are part of the launch in every pack. Priced once, whether or not a migration runs beside it. Shopify holds 100,000 redirects per store, 20 million on Plus — what sets the work is building the map, not the platform’s limit.
addons.$comment: Was a comparison row promising M and L up to ten thousand URLs that neither band paid for: taking it moved a full pack past its ceiling (audit N3, C11). As an add-on it is priced where it is bought, and the boundary is above ten thousand, as the name says.

addons.description: Selling on a recurring basis: Shopify Subscriptions with selling plans, the storefront widget, the customer portal and the billing states the support team has to recognise — or a third-party app where prepaid, build-a-box, B2B or international plans are needed, with live contracts carried across without the customer re-entering a card.
addons.note: Not in any pack, and not a plan question: Shopify Subscriptions runs from Basic. What decides the tier is whether the plans go past what it does.

addons.what: Blocks after the sale, inside the checkout steps, or Functions
addons.description: The checkout past what each pack configures: in S, blocks on the Thank you and Order status pages; below L, UI extensions and custom fields inside the information, shipping and payment steps (Shopify Plus); and in every pack, backend logic as Shopify Functions — validation, delivery and payment customisation, order rules.
addons.note: Blocks on the Thank you and Order status pages are already in Ecommerce Scale and Ecommerce Flagship. Inside the checkout steps is Shopify Plus only (rule 11.1), and a fully custom checkout UI is not sold at all (rule 11.6).

addons.description: A promotion Shopify’s own discounts cannot express, built as a discount Function the client owns: tiered or volume discounts for consumers, or stacking rules of the business’s own across discounts. Shopify’s own discounts are in every pack.
addons.note: A custom app containing a Function needs Shopify Plus; below Plus the Function comes in a public App Store app, which runs on every plan. Several product discounts on the same item is Shopify Plus only, and a setting there rather than a Function.

addons.what: Agentic commerce: data mapping, a crawler policy, or the store’s own assistant
addons.description: What takes a build past the AI every pack includes: product data mapped from custom fields into Shopify Catalog, an AI crawler policy, or the store’s own shopping assistant built on its Storefront MCP endpoint.
addons.note: Products in AI assistants, the Knowledge Base answers and Shopify Magic and Sidekick are in every pack. Parts of Shopify’s agent tooling are early access — the Universal Cart API — and are scoped rather than promised. A model’s running cost is the client’s, like an app’s fee.

addons.what: More destinations, a tag manager or consent
addons.description: Measurement past Shopify Analytics and GA4: customer events, the destinations wired through them and consent respected on each — and, at the advanced tier, server-side tagging or a third-party consent platform with the reconciliation that proves the numbers still line up.

addons.what: Written SOPs, or a handover into a retainer
addons.description: The operating model past the hypercare every pack carries: the runbooks the client’s team runs the store from, an owner named against each, and the handover into a retainer that has to receive it.
addons.note: The Grow retainer itself is offered with every pack after launch, its price kept open; the handover into it, once signed, is part of it.
